papers.summary: S-SALAAD jointly trains dense, low-rank, and structured-sparse weight components for compression to multiple deployment budgets. Its low-rank-only variant gives a better reported perplexity–compressibility trade-off than direct nuclear-norm regularization.
papers.relevance: The closest match to training weights for later low-rank compression, with a direct comparison to spectral regularization. Reported memory and throughput gains concern inference, not training.

evidence.quote: L L -only S-SALAAD maintains low perplexity over the same budget range, providing a better trade-off between model quality and elastic compressibility than these direct regularization baselines.
These measurements characterize prefill computation and do not include autoregressive decoding or complete request latency.

papers.title: Learning Structured Sparsity for Large Models: Bridging Model Compressibility and Efficient Inference

papers.summary: The paper attributes instability at large asymmetric LoRA learning-rate ratios to initialization-induced noise and proposes a smaller-variance initialization. It reports a wider stable learning-rate region across ranks and update multipliers.
papers.relevance: Directly informs LoRA optimization and hyperparameter selection in practical language-model fine-tuning.

evidence.quote: Empirically, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers.
The LLM experiments cover both encoder-only models (RoBERTa-base on GLUE) and decoder-only models (Llama arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks, with additional backbones in the appendix).

papers.title: Rethinking LoRA Initialization for Robust Asymmetric Learning Rates

papers.summary: On matrix quadratics, the paper analyzes when Muon's polar update helps or slows optimization. It argues that a finite number of Newton–Schulz steps can handle tiny singular modes better than exact orthogonalization, then measures such modes in a Muon-trained transformer.
papers.relevance: A close match for matrix optimization, Muon, Newton–Schulz approximations, and singular-value dynamics. Its transformer run is diagnostic, not a reported head-to-head LLM training benchmark.

evidence.quote: Finally, the few Newton--Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon , about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

We trained a decoder-only transformer with Muon and saved, at 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of training, the weights, the momentum matrices M M , and the raw minibatch gradients G G of all 50 matrices trained by Muon .

papers.title: A Quadratic Lens on Muon's Polar Update: Benefits, Pitfalls, and the Role of Newton-Schulz

papers.summary: LEMS allocates ranks across layers and KFAC-SVD changes the decomposition objective. Reported comparisons cover Mistral, Llama 3, and Qwen3; LEMS improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy across the evaluated Qwen3 sizes and compression ratios.
papers.relevance: Provides model-quality versus low-rank compression evidence across scales, though it studies post-training compression rather than training for compressibility.

evidence.quote: Table 2 details the results for all approaches under uniform compression rates (0.9, 0.7) and calibration sample count, with an additional line for our search-enhanced variant.
Averaged over ratios and models, it reduces perplexity by 17% for KFAC-SVD and 34% for SVD-LLM , while increasing zero-shot accuracy by +7.2 and +9.1 p.p. , respectively.

papers.title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search

papers.summary: In a noisy CIFAR-10 task, larger, deeper networks attain their best observed test performance after fitting the randomly labeled examples, unlike fixed-feature and shallower models. A separate kernel-gradient-flow analysis gives a phase diagram for when early stopping helps.
papers.relevance: Directly addresses memorization and generalization under label noise, while distinguishing the neural-network observation from the narrower kernel theory.

evidence.quote: Figure 1 shows that the larger and deeper networks attain their best observed test performance only after their memorization error reaches zero, while fixed-feature and shallower models exhibit late-time test-error deterioration.

Our analysis does not, however, establish that the networks learn this same geometry, nor does it explain how feature learning, architecture, and optimization produce the empirically observed behavior.

papers.title: When is early stopping beneficial under label noise? A phase diagram for kernel gradient flow

papers.summary: A controlled agent study compares receiving a scientific tool's report inline with retrieving it through an index. Some models lose accuracy under retrieval because they answer from self-created output rather than the canonical report.
papers.relevance: Offers a concrete failure mode for a handwritten research-digest harness that retrieves passages and requires source-grounded answers.

evidence.quote: The simulation, the tools, and the step budget are the same in all of them.
Under TOC, GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 skip the report in more than half of their trajectories: no part of it reaches them.

papers.title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy

papers.summary: The paper applies post-hoc singular-value smoothing and spiking to transformer feed-forward projections in five Llama and Qwen instruction models. It reports non-uniform changes across evaluated tasks, with sensitivity varying by model and layerwise spectrum.
papers.relevance: Direct evidence that altering LLM weight spectra can change task behavior, relevant to assessing quality costs of spectral regularization and compression. It does not test a training regularizer.

evidence.quote: We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices.

The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality.

papers.title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models

limitations: No selected paper establishes a quality–peak-training-memory–throughput–communication trade-off for memory-efficient LLM pretraining; focused searches did not surface a direct match among screened candidates.
S-SALAAD's quoted peak-memory and throughput measurements describe inference prefill, not training.
The Muon paper's main controlled results are on matrix quadratics; the inspected transformer run does not establish a comparative LLM training-speed gain.
The agent evidence-retrieval experiment uses a deterministic simulator, so transfer to paper-digest workflows remains untested.
X analysis was disabled; code availability and reproducibility were not checked.
